summary: This RFC defines a YANG data model for managing PCEP, covering communication between a Path Computation Client and Element, or between two PCEs.

plainLanguage.summary: A standard settings form for path-planning computers, so tools can configure and check them the same way.

subtitle: A standard YANG data model for configuring and monitoring PCEP, the protocol routers use to ask a path computation server for routes.

tldr.problem: PCEP speakers (path computation clients and elements) need a common way to be identified, configured and monitored, instead of each vendor using its own proprietary model.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two YANG 1.1 modules: ietf-pcep for configuration and state of the local entity, its peers and sessions, and ietf-pcep-stats, which augments it with counters and telemetry. Notifications and RPCs cover session events and resynchronization.
tldr.outcome: Management tools can configure and inspect PCEP devices the same way, and the model maps back to the existing PCEP MIB. Segment Routing over IPv6 is left to a separate module.

today: RFC 9826 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2025 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. IANA registered both YANG module names and their XML namespaces for it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes a network path from a network graph and constraints. A Path Computation Client (PCC) asks it for paths. PCEP, defined in RFC 5440, is the protocol they use. Its extensions cover stateful control of MPLS-TE Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in RFC 8231 and Segment Routing in RFC 8664 and RFC 9603.

RFC 9826 defines a YANG 1.1 data model for managing PCEP speakers, so that how they are identified, configured and monitored is common. It holds both configuration data and state data. Two modules are specified: ietf-pcep and ietf-pcep-stats. Both follow the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) of RFC 8342.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper form for network path planners now has an official layout, with one page for settings and a second page for counting what they do.

sections.title: Terminology and Conventions
sections.content:
The document builds on terms from RFC 4655, RFC 5440, RFC 7420, RFC 8051, RFC 8231 and RFC 8281. A PCEP entity is a local PCEP speaker and a PCEP peer is a remote one. Other terms it uses include stateful, passive and active PCE, delegation, PLSP-ID, Path Setup Type and PCE-initiated LSPs.

Data model diagrams use the tree notation of RFC 8340. Names are written without a prefix when the module is clear, and otherwise with standard prefixes such as inet, yang, te-types, key-chain, nacm, tlss, tlsc, ospf and isis. A table lists the many PCEP-related RFCs that the module references, for example for objective functions, associations, hierarchical PCE and TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using the form, the RFC explains the words on it and the short names for the other forms it borrows from.

sections.title: The ietf-pcep Data Model
sections.content:
The top of the model is a pcep container holding one entity, the local PCEP speaker. The entity has an IP address and a mandatory role, plus domains, capabilities, authentication settings, PCE information and many timers such as dead-timer and keepalive-timer. YANG timer names use hyphens, so DeadTimer from RFC 5440 becomes dead-timer. When the entity is a PCE it can also hold path-key and LSP database information.

Beneath the entity is a flat peer list, keyed by IP address. A speaker with several addresses looks like several peers. The list includes configured peers and ones learned dynamically, for instance through IGP discovery. Because sessions can be ephemeral, a peer is tracked even without a current session, and its statistics are the total across successive sessions. An implementation MAY discard this information only if no session exists for the peer.

Each peer holds a flat session list, keyed by the initiator. RFC 5440 forbids more than one active session between two entities, but during setup one session started locally and one started by the peer can briefly exist, and the one that does not reach the active state is discarded. Session data is for the current session only.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one card for the machine itself, a stack of cards for each machine it talks to, and a small card for each current conversation.

sections.title: Notifications, RPCs and Statistics
sections.content:
The model defines notifications for important protocol events, covering those of the PCEP MIB in RFC 7420: pcep-session-up, pcep-session-down, local overload and its clear, and peer overload and its clear. There is one RPC, trigger-resync, which asks a PCE to resynchronize state with a particular PCC as a sanity check.

The separate ietf-pcep-stats module augments the base module with statistics at both the peer and the session level. These include message counters such as PCReq, PCRep, PCErr, PCNtf and keepalives sent and received, response time measures, and counters for SVEC, stateful, PCE-initiated and path-key operations. Statistics can be reset with a reset-statistics action on a peer or session, or with the RPC reset-pcep-statistics-all where supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The form can ring a bell when a conversation starts or stops or when a machine is overloaded, and a second page keeps tally marks that can be wiped clean.

sections.title: Advanced PCE Features and TLS
sections.content:
Beyond the basics, the base module handles capability and scope, local and neighbor domain information, path-key, objective functions, Global Concurrent Optimization, point-to-multipoint, GMPLS, inter-layer, stateful PCE, Segment Routing for MPLS, authentication including TLS, and hierarchical PCE. Segment Routing over IPv6 is out of scope; the RFC points to a separate PCEP-SRv6 YANG module.

For a stateful PCE, the operational datastore keeps an LSP-DB of LSP state, keyed by the PLSP-ID, the PCC address and the LSP-ID. It holds PCEP-specific attributes, while generic traffic engineering attributes are defined in a separate TE model that it references.

For PCEPS (PCEP over TLS), RFC 8253 describes TLS 1.2 or later and a further document covers TLS 1.3. The PCC acts as TLS client and the PCE as TLS server, and StartTLS runs before any PCEP messages so identity is verified before the session is established. The module uses the TLS groupings of RFC 9645. TLS 1.2 can still be enabled with the tls12 feature, even though that feature is marked deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: The form also has optional pages for special jobs, like keeping a list of every route being managed and turning on secure, locked conversations.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules are meant to be accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF over a secure transport with mutual authentication, with access limited by the NETCONF Access Control Model (NACM, RFC 8341). Writable nodes such as /pcep/entity/ and /pcep/entity/peers are sensitive: unauthorized changes can disrupt PCEP sessions and lead to an inability to compute new paths.

Some readable data is sensitive too. The LSP database shows all LSPs in the network, which could reveal path and network usage, and path-keys hide Confidential Path Segments, so access could leak confidential path information. The trigger-resync RPC could force a session into continuous state synchronization if misused. Authentication key data must be kept secret, because its compromise lets an attacker forge PCEP traffic. Implementations must rate-limit notifications to avoid a notification flood.

For ietf-pcep-stats, no writable or readable data nodes are especially sensitive, but reset-pcep-statistics-all could impact monitoring if used without authorization.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted people should be allowed to change the settings or peek at the route list, because misuse could break connections or leak secrets.

sections.title: Example and Relationship to the MIB
sections.content:
Appendix B gives a JSON example of a PCE with addresses 192.0.2.3 and 2001:db8::3 serving PCCs at 192.0.2.1, 192.0.2.2 and 2001:db8::4. It shows the entity's role and timers, two delegated LSPs in the LSP database, and peers with remotely initiated sessions.

The design objectives in Appendix C ask for a simple model that is usable as is by new implementations, maps clearly to the PCEP MIB, allows static peers, includes read-only counters, and is easy to augment. Appendix D maps YANG nodes to PCEP MIB objects of RFC 7420; for example /pcep/entity corresponds to PcePcepEntityEntry and each peer to a pcePcepPeerEntry.
sections.plainLanguage: The back of the RFC shows a filled-in form for one planner talking to three routers, and a chart matching each new field to the old form it replaces.
